title: Va'era: four promises (Exodus 6:6–7)
hookLine: I will bring out, deliver, redeem and take; the four cups of the seder

cards: If you've been to a Passover seder, you know there's wine. A lot of it, or grape juice, poured four separate times at set points in the evening. Kids count the cups.
Grandparents mutter about the fourth one. Some families set an extra cup in the middle of the table that nobody drinks, and open the door for it later in the night. Why four?
Why the fifth? The answer isn't in the Passover story itself. It's in a few lines God says to Moses, right after Moses's angry complaint.

teach.b: This portion is called Va'era, and I appeared, from God's words: I appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Then God gives Moses a message for the people, a chain of verbs.
In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians." I will deliver you from their bondage. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm.
And: "I will take you to Me for a people." In Hebrew, vehotzeti, vehitzalti, vega'alti, velakachti.
Bring out, deliver, redeem, take. They build. First, out from under the burden: the work stops.
Then out of slavery itself. Then redeemed, bought back, restored. And last, not just free from something, but taken toward someone: you'll be my people.
Freedom isn't only escape. It ends in belonging.
The rabbis of the Jerusalem Talmud connected these four verbs to the four cups of wine at the seder, one cup for each promise. So every Passover, families drink their way, slowly, through this verse.

teach.h: THE FIFTH CUP WAITS FOR ELIJAH.
teach.b: And the fifth cup? The very next verse has a fifth promise: I will bring you in, to the land. Some texts of the Talmud mention a fifth cup, and later sages debated it.
One popular explanation: the question was left for the prophet Elijah to settle someday, so a cup is poured for him, and nobody drinks it.
Four promises kept at the table, and one still waiting at the door.

how: At the Passover seder, each participant drinks four cups of wine or grape juice at set points in the evening, and a cup is customarily poured for Elijah, with the door opened for him near the end of the meal.

I will redeem, one of God's four promises

games.q: four promises, four cups — tap the pairs.
p: I will take you to Me

s: the four cups are commanded in the Exodus story itself
the rabbis linked them to the four promises of Exodus 6:6–7; the custom is rabbinic.
there's a fifth promise in the next verse
I will bring you in, to the land. some connect it to the cup for Elijah.
from God's words: I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob.

games.q: Moses has just shouted at God: why have you harmed this people? what comes back?
o: a chain of promises: bring out, deliver, redeem, take.
games.why: God answered with four promises. the last one isn't about escape but belonging: I will take you to Me for a people.

practice: Count four freedoms on your fingers, one per breath or so: a burden you've been brought out from, something you're free of that once held you, something restored to you, and a place or person you belong to now.
They can be small: a debt paid, a habit dropped, a friendship repaired, a table where you're welcome.
